title: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection
hook: a sister ties a thread on her brother's wrist, and he promises to look after her
carry: a thread can hold a promise
tomorrow: Janmashtami: the night Krishna was born

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shivaratri: a hunter up a tree, awake all night. Your line was stay awake for what matters. Where did you stay three breaths longer? Today, the smallest festival object there is: a thread. Day eighty-four.

It's a summer morning, the full moon of the month of Shravana. In homes across India and far beyond, a sister sets out a small plate: a little lamp, a pinch of red powder, a few sweets, and a thread. Sometimes it's a plain red and gold string. Sometimes it's a glittering thing with a plastic cartoon on it, because her brother is six. She marks his forehead, circles the lamp in front of his face, ties the thread around his wrist, and pops a sweet in his mouth. He gives her a gift, and a promise: I'll look after you. Brothers who live on other continents get their threads in the mail.
screen: `A PLATE, A LAMP, A THREAD.` → `TIED AROUND HIS WRIST.` → `I'LL LOOK AFTER YOU.`

segments.voice: The name tells you what it is. Raksha means protection. Bandhan means a tie, a bond. Raksha Bandhan: the tie of protection. The thread itself is called a rakhi. What's surprising is how small it is. It isn't a contract. It won't hold anything up. You could snap it with two fingers. And yet people keep these threads on for days, sometimes until they fray off, because of what it holds. The best-known story behind it isn't really in the old texts, and it's worth saying so. People tell that Krishna once cut his finger, and Draupadi, without a second thought, tore a strip from the edge of her sari and tied it around the wound. Krishna was moved, and promised to protect her. Years later, in the Mahabharata, Draupadi is dragged into a hall full of men and humiliated, and her sari is pulled. And the cloth doesn't end. It keeps coming, more and more of it, and she's covered. The Mahabharata tells the endless cloth; the torn strip and the promise are how many families tell why. A strip of cloth for a strip of cloth. Notice which way it runs. The one who ties the thread isn't asking for charity. She's offering care first, and the promise answers it. In many families today the thread goes both ways: sisters tie it on sisters, cousins, close friends. And that's the week. A birth at midnight, a clay god welcomed home, nine nights of the Goddess, a row of lamps, a fire and then colors, a night awake, and now a thread.
screen: `RAKSHA — PROTECTION. BANDHAN — A TIE.` · `SMALL ENOUGH TO SNAP.` · `A STRIP OF CLOTH FOR A STRIP OF CLOTH.` · `CARE FIRST, THEN THE PROMISE.` · then, large: `A THREAD CAN HOLD A PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one person you'd protect. Settle, and breathe. Let a face come. A sibling, a child, a parent getting older, a friend having a rough year. Picture tying a thread around their wrist, slowly, the way it's done. Then say it inside, in your own words: I've got you. Stay with their face for a few breaths. Then decide how you'll tell them, today. A text is fine. The bell holds the time.
Rakhi. The thread tied on Raksha Bandhan, the tie of protection. Small enough to snap, strong enough to hold a promise.
Your line: a thread can hold a promise. Today, tell the person you pictured that you've got them. Then keep one small thread on your wrist, or in your mind, to remind you. Day eighty-four.
